file_name: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf

sections.title: Root
sections.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root

children.title: Abstract
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Abstract
children.summary: The abstract introduces Toolformer, a model trained to decide which APIs to call and how to incorporate their results into future token prediction. It is trained in a self-supervised way using only a handful of demonstrations per API. The model incorporates tools such as a calculator, Q&A system, search engine, translation system, and calendar, achieving substantially improved zero-shot performance across various downstream tasks.

children.title: 1 Introduction
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/1 Introduction
children.summary: The Introduction section outlines the limitations of current large language models, such as their inability to access up-to-date information, tendency to hallucinate facts, and lack of mathematical skills. It proposes 'Toolformer', a model that learns to use external tools like search engines and calculators in a self-supervised manner without requiring extensive human annotations.

children.title: 2 Approach
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/2 Approach
children.summary: The page presents a method for equipping language models with tool-use capabilities via API calls. It details an approach using in-context learning to generate datasets of potential API calls, which are then filtered based on their utility for predicting future tokens. The text includes Figure 2, illustrating the three-step process: sampling API calls, executing them, and filtering them. It also references prior work such as Toolformer (Wang and Komatsuzaki, 2021) and GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020).

children.title: Sampling API Calls
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/2 Approach/Sampling API Calls
children.summary: The section describes the process of sampling API calls for a Question Answering task. It involves writing a prompt P(x) to encourage a Language Model (LM) to annotate text with API calls. The method calculates the probability p_i of starting an API call at each position i in the sequence. A sampling threshold τ_s is used to filter positions, keeping those where p_i > τ_s. If more than k positions are kept, only the top k are selected. Finally, up to m API calls are sampled for each selected position using the model M.

children.title: Executing API Calls
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/2 Approach/Executing API Calls
children.summary: This section describes the process of executing API calls generated by a model M. It explains that execution methods vary depending on the specific API, such as calling another neural network, running a Python script, or using a retrieval system. The output for each call must be formatted as a single text sequence.

children.title: Filtering API Calls
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/2 Approach/Filtering API Calls
children.summary: The section 'Filtering API Calls' describes a method to determine whether an API call is helpful for the model. It defines a weighted cross-entropy loss function and compares two scenarios: one where the API call and its result are provided as a prefix, and another where no API call is made or only the input is provided. The text explains that an API call is considered helpful if providing it reduces the loss by at least a specific threshold (τf).

children.title: Model Finetuning
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/2 Approach/Model Finetuning
children.summary: The section describes the final step of the process, which is Model Finetuning. It explains that after sampling and filtering API calls for all APIs, the remaining calls are merged with the original text to create a new training sequence. This involves interleaving the API call and its result into the input text at the specific position where the call was made.

children.title: 3 Tools
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/3 Tools
children.summary: Section 3 describes five tools used to augment regular language models: a question answering system (Atlas), a calculator, a Wikipedia search engine (BM25), a machine translation system (NLLB), and a calendar API. The section details the specific implementations and constraints for each tool.

children.title: 4 Experiments
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/4 Experiments
children.summary: Section 4.1 Experimental Setup describes the dataset generation process for the experiments. It specifies that a subset of CCNet is used as the language modeling dataset (C) and GPT-J is used as the language model (M). To reduce annotation costs, heuristics are defined to select subsets of C where API calls are likely to be helpful.

children.title: Appendix A
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A

children.title: Baseline Models
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A/Baseline Models
children.summary: The section describes the baseline models used for comparison, including GPT-J (unfinetuned), GPT-J + CC (finetuned on a subset of CCNet without API calls), Toolformer (finetuned on a subset of CCNet augmented with API calls), and Toolformer (disabled) where API calls are disabled during decoding. It also mentions comparisons to larger models OPT (66B) and GPT-3 (175B).

children.title: 4.2 Downstream Tasks
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A/4.2 Downstream Tasks
children.summary: Section 4.2 describes the evaluation setup for downstream tasks, focusing on a prompted zero-shot approach where models are instructed to solve tasks in natural language without provided examples. It contrasts this with prior work that uses dataset-specific examples and mentions comparisons against larger baseline models like OPT (66B) and GPT-3 (175B). The section also details the use of standard greedy decoding with a specific modification for Toolformer.

children.title: 4.2.1 LAMA
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A/4.2 Downstream Tasks/4.2.1 LAMA
children.summary: Section 4.2.1 evaluates the Toolformer model on the LAMA benchmark, specifically using the SQuAD, Google-RE, and T-REx subsets to test fact completion tasks. The text explains that examples were filtered to ensure the mask token is the final token and that the Wikipedia Search API was disabled for Toolformer to prevent unfair advantages. Table 3 presents results showing that Toolformer significantly outperforms baseline models like GPT-J and larger models like OPT (66B) and GPT-3 (175B), achieving competitive scores with GPT-3 (175B). The section attributes this success to the model's ability to independently decide to use a question answering tool in almost all cases.

children.title: 4.2.2 Math Datasets
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A/4.2 Downstream Tasks/4.2.2 Math Datasets
children.summary: Section 4.2.2 Math Datasets evaluates the mathematical reasoning abilities of models on three benchmarks: ASDiv, SVAMP, and MAWPS. The section describes a zero-shot evaluation setup using a lenient criterion where the model's prediction is checked for containing the first number after an equals sign. Table 4 presents results showing that Toolformer significantly outperforms baseline models (GPT-J, OPT, GPT-3) by leveraging a calculator tool in 97.9% of cases.

children.title: 4.2.3 Question Answering
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A/4.2 Downstream Tasks/4.2.3 Question Answering
children.summary: Section 4.2.3 introduces the evaluation of question answering capabilities using three datasets: Web Questions, Natural Questions, and TriviaQA. The section specifies that for evaluation, the system checks if the correct answer is contained within the first 20 words predicted by the model rather than requiring an exact match. Additionally, it notes that for the Toolformer model, the question answering tool is disabled during this specific evaluation.

children.title: 4.2.4 Multilingual Question Answering
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A/4.2 Downstream Tasks/4.2.4 Multilingual Question Answering
children.summary: Section 4.2.4 evaluates Toolformer and baseline models on the MLQA multilingual question-answering benchmark, where context is in English but questions are in Arabic, German, Spanish, Hindi, Vietnamese, or Simplified Chinese. Results (Table 6) show that using a machine translation API consistently improves performance across languages, with Toolformer outperforming GPT-J baselines in most cases except for some languages where finetuning on CCNet causes deterioration. OPT and GPT-3 perform poorly due to lack of multilingual training data.

children.title: 4.2.5 Temporal Datasets
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A/4.2 Downstream Tasks/4.2.5 Temporal Datasets
children.summary: Section 4.2.5 Temporal Datasets introduces the evaluation of models on temporal datasets to investigate the utility of a calendar API. It describes two datasets: TEMPLAMA, which contains cloze queries about facts that change over time (e.g., 'Cristiano Ronaldo plays for ___') based on Wikidata for years between 2010 and 2020; and DATESET, a new dataset generated using templates with random dates/durations (e.g., 'What day of the week was it 30 days ago?'). Both require knowledge of the current date to answer correctly.

children.title: 4.3 Language Modeling
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A/4.3 Language Modeling
children.summary: Section 4.3 discusses the language modeling performance of the Toolformer model to ensure it does not degrade during finetuning with API calls. The authors evaluate their models on two datasets: WikiText and a subset of CCNet. Table 8 presents perplexity results for various models (GPT-J, GPT-J + CC, Toolformer) on these datasets, showing that adding API calls does not increase perplexity compared to training without them.

children.title: 4.4 Scaling Laws
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/Appendix A/4.4 Scaling Laws
children.summary: Section 4.4 investigates how the ability to use external tools affects performance as the size of the language model (LM) increases. The authors apply their approach to four smaller models from the GPT-2 family (124M, 355M, 775M, and 1.6B parameters) alongside GPT-J, using a subset of three tools: question answering, calculator, and Wikipedia search. The section reports that leveraging provided tools only emerges at around 775M parameters; smaller models perform similarly with or without tools. It is hypothesized that the Wikipedia search API is an exception because it is easy to use. As models grow larger, they improve at solving tasks both with and without API calls, but a large gap remains between predictions made with and without API calls even for the largest model.

children.title: 5 Analysis
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/5 Analysis
children.summary: The section titled '5 Analysis' begins by introducing a subsection on 'Decoding Strategy', which investigates the effects of a modified decoding strategy previously introduced in Section 4.2. The text explains that this strategy involves generating tokens differently than always generating the most probable one, though the full explanation is cut off at the bottom of the page.

children.title: 6 Related Work
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/6 Related Work
children.summary: This page presents experimental results and analysis regarding a model called Toolformer. Figure 4 displays line charts comparing the performance of Toolformer, Toolformer with disabled API calls, and GPT3 across LAMA, Math Benchmarks, and QA Benchmarks as model parameters increase. Table 9 details Toolformer's performance on T-REx and WebQS datasets for different values of k (the number of most likely tokens considered), showing metrics for overall performance, API call success, and non-call accuracy. The text discusses how increasing k leads to more API calls and improved performance, particularly on WebQS. A section titled 'Data Quality' qualitatively analyzes API calls generated by the approach, referencing Table 10 (not fully visible) and discussing filtering criteria based on score differences. The page concludes with the beginning of Section 6, 'Related Work,' which introduces approaches to augment language models with textual information during pretraining.

children.title: Tool Use
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/6 Related Work/Tool Use
children.summary: The section discusses approaches to equip language models (LMs) with the ability to use external tools such as search engines, web browsers, calculators, translation systems, and Python interpreters. It categorizes learning methods into those relying on large amounts of human supervision versus few-shot prompting setups. It also mentions TALM as a related self-supervised approach.

children.title: Bootstrapping
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/6 Related Work/Bootstrapping
children.summary: The section titled 'Bootstrapping' discusses the concept of using self-training and bootstrapping techniques to improve models. It lists various contexts where these methods have been investigated, including word sense disambiguation, relation extraction, parsing, sequence generation, and few-shot text classification.

children.title: 7 Limitations
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/7 Limitations
children.summary: The section outlines several limitations of the Toolformer approach. Key issues include the inability to use tools in a chain (using one tool's output as another's input) because API calls are generated independently, and the lack of support for interactive tool usage like search engines. Additionally, models are sensitive to prompt wording, the method is sample-inefficient (requiring large datasets for few examples), and it does not account for the computational cost of making API calls.

children.title: 8 Conclusion
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/8 Conclusion
children.summary: The section introduces Toolformer, a language model designed to learn self-supervised usage of various tools like search engines and calculators through simple API calls. The model is finetuned on sampled API calls filtered by their ability to reduce perplexity on future tokens. It is noted that Toolformer significantly improves zero-shot performance compared to larger models.

children.title: A API Details
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/A API Details

children.title: A.1 Implementation
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/A API Details/A.1 Implementation
children.summary: Section A.1 Implementation details the specific models and tools used for four tasks: Question Answering (Atlas model), Calculator (Python script with basic operators), Calendar (date extraction from URLs), and Machine Translation (600M parameter NLLB). It also describes data filtering heuristics applied to the CCNet dataset, such as language detection using fastText and token chunking.

children.title: A.2 Prompts
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/A API Details/A.2 Prompts
children.summary: Section A.2 lists the specific prompts used to sample API calls for the Question Answering and Calculator tools. For Question Answering, the prompt instructs the model to add API calls to text to answer questions, providing examples of input/output pairs involving Joe Biden and Coca-Cola. For the Calculator tool, the prompt begins by defining the task as adding calls to a Calculator API.

children.title: Wikipedia Search
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/A API Details/A.2 Prompts/Wikipedia Search
children.summary: The section titled 'Wikipedia Search' explains how to use a Wikipedia Search API to look up information. It provides examples of input prompts and corresponding outputs, such as searching for the meaning of colors on the Ghana flag and risks associated with nanomaterial production.

children.title: Machine Translation
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/A API Details/A.2 Prompts/Machine Translation
children.summary: The section titled 'Machine Translation' explains how to use a Machine Translation API. It instructs the user to complete text by using the tool with the syntax '[MT(text)]', where 'text' is the input to be translated into English. The section provides three examples: translating a book title from Portuguese, translating a German phrase about Morris de Jonge's work, and translating Chinese text regarding Gaochun district in Nanjing.

children.title: Calendar
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/A API Details/A.2 Prompts/Calendar
children.summary: This section explains the usage of a Calendar API tool designed to add calls for processing text. It provides instructions on how to invoke the API using the syntax "[Calendar()]" and includes an example where the input 'Today is the first Friday of the year' is processed.

children.title: B Toolformer Training
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/B Toolformer Training
children.summary: The section details the training configuration for Toolformer, specifying a maximum of 25k examples per API, a sequence length of 1,024, and an effective batch size of 128. It notes that models are trained using DeepSpeed's ZeRO-3 on 8 NVIDIA A100 40GB GPUs with BF16 precision. The training runs for up to 2k steps, evaluating perplexity (PPL) every 500 steps on a small development set from CCNet containing 1,000 examples.

children.title: C Zero-Shot Prompts
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/C Zero-Shot Prompts

children.title: C.1 LAMA and TEMPLAMA
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/C Zero-Shot Prompts/C.1 LAMA and TEMPLAMA
children.summary: Section C.1 describes the zero-shot prompt used for both LAMA and TEMPLAMA tasks. The prompt instructs the model to complete an input text 'x' so that it is factually correct.

children.title: C.2 Math Benchmarks
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/C Zero-Shot Prompts/C.2 Math Benchmarks
children.summary: Section C.2 Math Benchmarks describes the prompt format used for math benchmarks, which involves providing a context (x) and a question (q) followed by 'The answer is.'

children.title: C.3 Question Answering
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/C Zero-Shot Prompts/C.3 Question Answering
children.summary: Section C.3 describes the prompt format used for question answering datasets, including DATESET. The method involves prefixing the question with 'Answer the following question:' and appending a question mark if one is not already present.

children.title: C.4 Multilingual Question Answering
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/C Zero-Shot Prompts/C.4 Multilingual Question Answering
children.summary: Section C.4 describes the prompt format used for Multilingual Question Answering (MLQA). It specifies that given a context x and a question q, the task is to answer the question in English.

children.title: D DATESET
children.path: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.pdf/Root/D DATESET
children.summary: Section D describes the creation of the DATESET dataset. It involves randomly selecting 500 'current dates' and generating relative past/future dates within a four-year range to fill query templates found in Table 11. The section provides an example query ('How many days ago was August 14, 2020?') and explains that a Calendar tool is used to return the current date (e.g., 'Today is Sunday, November 20, 2020').
